title: Who Owned a Career
bigQuestion: When a team can trade a player's name without asking, who owns that player's career, and how did players win part of it back?

story.title: A Phone Call in October
story.kicker: A star learns from a phone call that his career now belongs to another city.
paragraphs: October 1969. Curt Flood has played center field for the St. Louis Cardinals for twelve seasons. He has won seven straight Gold Glove awards and played in three World Series. He owns a home and a portrait business in St. Louis. Then a club official calls to tell him he has been traded to the Philadelphia Phillies.

Flood was not asked. The trade was a seven-player deal, and the Cardinals received the slugger Dick Allen. Flood's contract, like every major-league contract, carried the reserve clause. That clause let a club renew a player's contract year after year. A player could not offer his work to any other club unless his team traded, sold or released him.

Flood did not want to go. He met with Marvin Miller, head of the Major League Baseball Players Association. Miller told him a lawsuit would likely fail and would probably end his career. The union's leaders agreed to pay his legal costs.

On December 24, 1969, Flood wrote to baseball commissioner Bowie Kuhn. He said that after twelve years in the major leagues he did not feel he was a piece of property to be bought and sold against his wishes. He asked to be free to hear offers from other clubs. Kuhn said no.

Flood sued in January 1970. He sat out the whole 1970 season rather than report to Philadelphia. His case would reach the United States Supreme Court. The question it asked was older than Flood himself: who owns a ballplayer's working life?
story.think: Flood was well paid. Why might a well-paid worker still object to being traded without being asked?

lessons.title: Five Names on a Reserve List
lessons.mainIdea: The National League, founded in 1876, began the reserve system in 1879, letting each club keep players from signing with rivals.
reading: William Hulbert, an owner of the Chicago White Stockings, led the founding of the National League of Professional Base Ball Clubs. Club owners met in New York on February 2, 1876. Before this, players had run their own association and often jumped from team to team. The new league was run by club owners, not players.

Player salaries rose as clubs bid against each other for stars. In 1879 the owners agreed in secret that each club could *reserve* five players. No other club in the league would try to sign a reserved player. A *reserve clause* is a contract term that keeps a player tied to one club.

The list grew. By the late 1880s, clubs could reserve nearly their whole roster. The reserve clause was written into standard player contracts. A player's only way to a new team was a trade, a sale or a release by his club. Clubs could also sell a player's contract to another club for cash, and the player received none of that money.

Owners said the system kept costs down and stopped rich clubs from buying every star. Players said it held down wages and removed their choice of employer. That argument, over whether the system protected the league or only the owners, lasted almost a hundred years.

words.d: to claim a player so no other club in the league may sign him
a contract term that tied a player to one club, which could renew his contract each year
the professional baseball league founded by club owners in 1876

look.title: A Secret Agreement
look.text: 1879. The owners of the National League clubs agree that each club may name five of its players as reserved. The other clubs promise not to sign them. The players are not part of the agreement and are not asked.
look.prompt: Who gained bargaining power from this agreement, and who lost it? Why might the owners have kept it secret at first?

check.q: Who led the founding of the National League in 1876?
choices: William Hulbert of the Chicago White Stockings
check.why: Hulbert, a Chicago club owner, drove the league's founding in February 1876.

check.q: How many players could each club reserve in 1879?
check.why: The 1879 agreement let each club reserve five players.

check.q: What did a reserve clause do?
choices: It guaranteed a player a raise.
It let a player choose his team each year.
It tied a player to one club, which could renew his contract.
check.why: The clause let the club renew the player's contract and kept rivals from signing him.

lessons.title: "Is the Base-Ball Player a Chattel?"
lessons.mainIdea: John Montgomery Ward organized the first players' union in 1885 and led a players' league in 1890 to escape the reserve system.
reading: John Montgomery Ward was a star pitcher and shortstop who also earned a law degree from Columbia. In 1885 he helped found the Brotherhood of Professional Base Ball Players. It was the first union of professional ballplayers in the United States. It pushed back against salary caps and the sale of players between clubs.

In August 1887, Ward published an article in Lippincott's Magazine titled Is the Base-Ball Player a Chattel? A *chattel* is a piece of movable property. Ward argued that the reserve rule, first meant to protect clubs, had become a tool for buying and selling men. He said players had no voice in the price or the place.

When owners refused to change, the Brotherhood started its own league. The *Players' League* played the 1890 season with eight clubs, including one in Chicago. Players shared in ownership and profits. Many stars jumped from the National League to join it.

The Players' League lasted one season. Its backers lost money in a three-way fight with the National League and the American Association. Several of its financial backers sold out to the older league. The reserve system survived, and the players returned to their old clubs.

words.d: a piece of movable property that can be owned, bought and sold
the Brotherhood of Professional Base Ball Players, the first ballplayers' union, founded in 1885
a league partly owned by players that played only the 1890 season

look.title: Ward's Question
look.text: Ward wrote that the reserve rule had started as a way for clubs to protect themselves against each other. Over time, he argued, it became a way to hold players and sell them like goods, with no say in where they went or what the club was paid.
look.cite: John Montgomery Ward, "Is the Base-Ball Player a Chattel?", Lippincott's Monthly Magazine, August 1887
look.prompt: Why did Ward choose the word chattel for his title? What was he asking readers to see?

check.q: What did John Montgomery Ward found in 1885?
choices: the Brotherhood of Professional Base Ball Players
check.why: Ward helped found the Brotherhood, the first ballplayers' union.

check.q: What is a chattel?
check.why: Ward used the word to argue players were being treated as property.

check.q: What happened to the Players' League?
choices: It won a Supreme Court case.
check.why: The Players' League lost money and folded after the 1890 season.

lessons.title: A Rival League and a Court
lessons.mainIdea: In 1922 the Supreme Court ruled that baseball was not interstate commerce, giving it an exemption from antitrust law that protected the reserve clause.
reading: The Federal League challenged the two major leagues in 1914 and 1915. Its Chicago team, the Whales, played in a new park on the North Side built by owner Charles Weeghman. When the Federal League folded, Weeghman bought the Cubs and moved them there in 1916. That ballpark is known today as Wrigley Field.

Most Federal League owners settled with the major leagues. The Baltimore club did not. It sued, saying the major leagues had broken the Sherman Antitrust Act. In Federal Baseball Club v. National League, decided in 1922, the Supreme Court ruled against Baltimore. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. wrote the opinion.

Holmes wrote that putting on baseball exhibitions was a local business, not *interstate commerce*. Interstate commerce is trade that crosses state lines, which Congress may regulate. Travel between cities, he said, was only incidental to the games. The ruling gave baseball an *antitrust exemption*.

Meanwhile, the 1919 World Series scandal, in which Chicago White Sox players were accused of taking money from gamblers, shook the sport. Owners hired Kenesaw Mountain Landis, a federal judge in Chicago, as the first commissioner in 1920. A *commissioner* is the official the owners hire to govern a league. Landis banned eight White Sox players for life, even though a Chicago jury had acquitted them in 1921.

words.d: trade and business that crosses state lines, which Congress can regulate
a special status that keeps a business from being sued under antitrust law
the official hired by team owners to govern a league
a rival major league that played in 1914 and 1915

look.title: Supreme Court Rulings on Sport and Antitrust
rows: Federal Baseball Club v. National League
look.cite: United States Reports; Supreme Court opinions
look.prompt: How many years passed between the Federal Baseball ruling and Flood v. Kuhn? What does that gap say about how long a court ruling can last?

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Federal Baseball Club v. National League (1922)?
choices: The Federal League could join the majors.
Baseball was not interstate commerce under antitrust law.
check.why: Justice Holmes wrote that baseball exhibitions were not interstate commerce.

check.q: Which Chicago ballpark began as the home of a Federal League team?
check.why: Weeghman built the park for the Chicago Whales; the Cubs moved there in 1916.

check.q: Who was baseball's first commissioner?
check.why: Owners hired Landis, a federal judge in Chicago, in 1920.

lessons.title: Rube Foster's League
lessons.mainIdea: Shut out of the major leagues by a color line, Black players built the Negro National League in 1920, where contracts were harder to enforce.
reading: By the 1890s, organized baseball had pushed out its few Black players. No written rule said so. Owners kept an unwritten *color line*, an agreement to hire only white players. Black players formed their own teams and traveled widely to find games. Some of these barnstorming clubs played in a new town almost every day.

Andrew "Rube" Foster was a pitcher, manager and owner of the Chicago American Giants. In February 1920, he met with other team owners at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City, Missouri. They formed the Negro National League. Foster led it and wanted Black-owned clubs to control Black baseball.

Negro League clubs had contracts, but no court or commissioner backed them the way the majors' reserve clause was backed. Players often jumped to teams that paid more. In 1937, Satchel Paige and other stars left to play in the Dominican Republic for a team tied to dictator Rafael Trujillo. Leagues also played winter seasons in Cuba, Puerto Rico and Mexico.

Leagues rose and fell during the Great Depression. The Negro American League formed in 1937. The East-West All-Star Game, first played at Comiskey Park in Chicago in 1933, became the biggest yearly event in Black baseball. In 2020, Major League Baseball announced it would count seven major Negro Leagues from 1920 to 1948 as major leagues in its records.

words.d: an unwritten agreement to keep Black players out of white leagues
the league of Black-owned and Black teams founded by Rube Foster in 1920
leaving a team for another that pays more before a contract ends

look.title: A Contract Without a Court
look.text: A Negro League star signs with one club for the season. In spring an offer arrives from a team in the Dominican Republic that pays far more. No commissioner and no court ruling will force the star to stay. The club can protest, fine or blacklist him in its own league, but cannot stop him from sailing.
look.prompt: How does this case show both a freedom and a weakness that major-league players did not have?

check.q: Who founded the Negro National League in 1920?
check.why: Rube Foster of the Chicago American Giants led the February 1920 meeting in Kansas City.

check.q: What was baseball's color line?
choices: the painted line between the bases
a written rule in the Official Baseball Rules
an unwritten agreement to hire only white players
check.why: No rule was written; owners kept Black players out by agreement.

check.q: Where was the first East-West All-Star Game played in 1933?
check.why: The East-West game began at Comiskey Park in 1933.

lessons.title: Signing Away a Star
lessons.mainIdea: When the major leagues began signing Black players in 1945, Negro League owners were often paid little or nothing for the players they lost.
reading: In October 1945, Branch Rickey of the Brooklyn Dodgers signed Jackie Robinson to play for the club's Montreal farm team. Robinson had played the 1945 season for the Kansas City Monarchs. Rickey said Robinson had no binding contract with the Monarchs. He paid them nothing. Robinson played his first game for Brooklyn on April 15, 1947.

Negro League owners were caught in a hard place. They supported the end of the color line. They also saw their best players leave without payment. The Monarchs' owners protested but did not sue. A lawsuit would have made them look as if they were standing in the way of integration.

Effa Manley co-owned the Newark Eagles with her husband, Abe Manley. In 1947 Cleveland owner Bill Veeck signed Larry Doby from the Eagles. Veeck paid Manley 10,000 dollars. Doby became the first Black player in the American League in July 1947. Manley insisted that Negro League contracts deserved the same respect as major-league ones.

As the best players left, fans followed them to the major leagues. A second Negro National League, formed in 1933, closed after the 1948 season. The Negro American League lasted into the early 1960s. In 2006, Effa Manley became the first woman elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame.

words.d: a minor-league team that a major-league club uses to develop players
opening a group or place to people who had been kept out by race
an agreement that the law will enforce

look.title: Two Signings Side by Side
look.text: 1945: Brooklyn signs Jackie Robinson from the Kansas City Monarchs and pays the Monarchs nothing. 1947: Cleveland signs Larry Doby from the Newark Eagles and pays Effa Manley 10,000 dollars. Both men break a color line. Only one Negro League club is paid.
look.prompt: What argument did Effa Manley make about Negro League contracts? Why did the difference between these two signings matter to Black-owned clubs?

check.q: How much did the Dodgers pay the Kansas City Monarchs for Jackie Robinson?
check.why: Rickey said Robinson had no binding contract and paid the Monarchs nothing.

check.q: Who co-owned the Newark Eagles and demanded payment for Larry Doby?
check.why: Effa Manley co-owned the Eagles and received 10,000 dollars for Doby.

check.q: What honor did Effa Manley receive in 2006?
choices: She became the first Black commissioner.
She became the first woman elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame.
She won a Supreme Court case.
check.why: Manley was elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2006.

lessons.title: Drafts in Football and Hockey
lessons.mainIdea: Other leagues also limited where players could go: the NFL began a draft in 1936, and hockey owners punished Ted Lindsay for organizing players in 1957.
reading: A *draft* is a system in which teams take turns choosing new players, and the chosen player may sign only with that team. The National Football League held its first draft on February 8, 1936, in Philadelphia. It was proposed by Bert Bell, owner of the Philadelphia Eagles. The weakest team picked first.

The first player ever drafted was Jay Berwanger of the University of Chicago. In 1935 he had won the first Downtown Athletic Club Trophy, soon renamed the Heisman Trophy. Berwanger never played in the NFL. He could not agree on pay with the Chicago Bears, who got his rights by trade, and he went into business instead.

The NFL had its own limit on moving teams. The *Rozelle Rule*, begun in 1963 under commissioner Pete Rozelle, let the commissioner award players or draft picks to a team that lost a player who signed elsewhere. That made clubs slow to sign other teams' players. In 1976, in Mackey v. National Football League, a federal appeals court ruled that the Rozelle Rule broke antitrust law.

In hockey, Detroit Red Wings star Ted Lindsay helped start a players' association in 1957. Players wanted to see pension records and bargain over conditions. That summer, Detroit traded Lindsay to the Chicago Black Hawks, then one of the league's weakest teams. The effort collapsed. The National Hockey League Players' Association formed in 1967.

words.d: a system in which teams take turns choosing new players, who may then sign only with the team that chose them
the NFL rule from 1963 to 1976 that made a team compensate the club of a player it signed
a union or group that represents the players in a league

look.title: The First Pick Who Never Played
look.text: February 1936. The NFL's first draft gives the Philadelphia Eagles the first choice. They pick Jay Berwanger of the University of Chicago. The Eagles trade his rights to the Chicago Bears. Berwanger and the Bears cannot agree on a salary. He never plays a professional game.
look.prompt: What choices did Berwanger still have after the draft? What choice had the draft taken away?

check.q: Who was the first player chosen in the first NFL draft in 1936?
check.why: Jay Berwanger of the University of Chicago was the first pick.

check.q: What did the court decide in Mackey v. National Football League (1976)?
choices: The Rozelle Rule broke antitrust law.
Football was exempt from antitrust law.
Players could not form a union.
check.why: The Eighth Circuit ruled the Rozelle Rule an illegal restraint.

check.q: What happened to Ted Lindsay after he helped organize hockey players in 1957?
choices: Detroit traded him to the Chicago Black Hawks.
He won a lawsuit against the league.
He was elected union president in 1967.
check.why: Detroit traded Lindsay to Chicago, then a weak team, after his organizing.

lessons.title: A Steelworkers' Economist Takes Over
lessons.mainIdea: Marvin Miller turned the baseball players' association into a strong union after 1966, winning its first contract, grievance arbitration and a 1972 strike.
reading: The Major League Baseball Players Association formed in the 1950s, but it was weak. In 1966 players elected Marvin Miller as its first full-time executive director. Miller had been an economist for the United Steelworkers of America. He had no background in baseball. He did have long experience in *collective bargaining*.

In 1968, Miller and the owners signed the first collective bargaining agreement in professional sport. It raised the minimum major-league salary from 6,000 dollars to 10,000 dollars. The minimum had barely changed in twenty years. The agreement also set rules on pensions and expenses.

In 1970, the players won *grievance arbitration*. A grievance is a formal complaint that the contract was broken. Arbitration means a neutral person, not the commissioner, decides the dispute. This change would later give the players their biggest victory.

In April 1972, the players went on strike for 13 days over pension payments. A *strike* is when workers stop working to press their demands. It was the first league-wide strike in modern major-league baseball. The owners agreed to add money to the pension fund, and the season started late.

words.d: talks between a union and employers to agree on pay and working rules
a system in which a neutral person decides complaints that a contract was broken
when workers stop working together to press their demands
the lowest pay a league allows a player to receive

look.title: The Major-League Minimum Salary
look.prompt: By how much did the first contract raise the minimum? Who sets the minimum today, the owners alone or both sides?

check.q: What was Marvin Miller's job before he led the players' association?
check.why: Miller came from the United Steelworkers of America in 1966.

check.q: What did the first collective bargaining agreement in 1968 do to the minimum salary?
check.why: The 1968 agreement raised the minimum to 10,000 dollars.

check.q: What is grievance arbitration?
choices: a neutral person deciding complaints that a contract was broken
check.why: Arbitration gave disputes to a neutral person rather than the commissioner.

lessons.title: Flood v. Kuhn
lessons.mainIdea: Curt Flood challenged the reserve clause in court; in 1972 the Supreme Court ruled against him but called baseball's exemption an anomaly that only Congress could fix.
reading: Curt Flood sued baseball commissioner Bowie Kuhn in January 1970. His lawyer was Arthur Goldberg, a former Supreme Court justice. Flood argued the reserve clause broke antitrust law and bound him to one club against his will. He lost at trial in 1970 and on appeal.

Flood sat out 1970. In 1971 he played briefly for the Washington Senators, then left the game. His case reached the Supreme Court. Flood was one of the few players to challenge the system in public, and he received hate mail and threats while the case went on.

On June 19, 1972, the Court ruled 5 to 3 against Flood. Justice Harry Blackmun wrote the opinion. He called baseball's exemption an *anomaly*, meaning something odd that does not fit the rule. Other sports had no exemption. Yet the Court said it would not overturn a rule baseball had relied on for fifty years.

Blackmun wrote that if the exemption was wrong, *Congress* should change it. Congress did so in part in 1998, with the Curt Flood Act. That law says major-league players have the same antitrust rights over employment as other professional athletes. By then Flood had died, in 1997.

words.d: something odd or out of place that does not fit the usual rule
an earlier court ruling that later courts follow
the part of the U.S. government that writes federal laws
the 1998 federal law that ended baseball's antitrust exemption for major-league players' employment

look.title: Why the Court Did Not Overturn Its Own Ruling
look.text: The Court admits baseball's exemption makes little sense. Football, boxing and basketball have no such exemption. But baseball has built its business around the 1922 ruling for fifty years. The Court decides that Congress, not the justices, should change it.
look.prompt: What is the argument for following precedent even when a court thinks the old ruling was odd? What did that choice cost Flood?

check.q: How did the Supreme Court rule in Flood v. Kuhn?
choices: It refused to hear the case.
check.why: On June 19, 1972, the Court ruled 5 to 3 against Flood.

check.q: What does anomaly mean in Justice Blackmun's opinion?
choices: something odd that does not fit the usual rule
check.why: Blackmun called baseball's exemption an anomaly because other sports had none.

check.q: What did the Curt Flood Act of 1998 do?
choices: It created free agency in football.
It ended baseball's antitrust exemption for players' employment.
check.why: Congress gave major-league players the same antitrust rights as other athletes.

lessons.title: An Arbitrator Reads the Clause
lessons.mainIdea: In December 1975, arbitrator Peter Seitz ruled that the reserve clause bound a player for only one extra year, opening the way to free agency in 1976.
reading: The first crack came from a broken promise. Oakland Athletics owner Charles Finley failed to make a payment required in pitcher Catfish Hunter's contract. In December 1974, an arbitrator ruled Hunter a *free agent*, a player free to sign with any team. On December 31, 1974, Hunter signed with the New York Yankees for about 3.75 million dollars over five years.

Marvin Miller saw a larger case in the contract's own words. The reserve clause said a club could renew a contract for one year. Owners read that as a renewal that repeated forever. In 1975, pitchers Andy Messersmith of the Los Angeles Dodgers and Dave McNally of the Montreal Expos played the season without signing new contracts.

On December 23, 1975, arbitrator Peter Seitz ruled for both players. He read the clause to mean one renewal year only, not a chain of years. After that year, Messersmith and McNally were free. The owners fired Seitz right away, and a federal court upheld his decision in 1976.

Owners and players then bargained over a new system. The 1976 agreement let players with six years of major-league service become free agents. The reserve clause did not disappear, but it now held a player for a limited time. Average salaries rose sharply over the next decade.

words.d: a player whose contract has ended and who may sign with any team
a neutral person chosen to decide a dispute between two sides
a system that lets players sign with any team after a set period

look.title: One Year, Not Forever
look.text: Seitz found that the renewal clause gave the club the right to renew a contract for one year. Nothing in the agreement, he wrote, let the club keep renewing it year after year without the player's consent. Once that year ended, the player was no longer bound.
look.cite: Peter Seitz, arbitration decision in the Messersmith and McNally grievances, December 23, 1975
look.prompt: Seitz did not strike down the clause; he read it. How can reading a contract's exact words change who holds power?

check.q: Why did Catfish Hunter become a free agent in 1974?
choices: Oakland's owner failed to make a payment required by his contract.
Congress passed the Curt Flood Act.
check.why: Charles Finley broke Hunter's contract by failing to make a required payment.

check.q: What did Peter Seitz rule in December 1975?
choices: The reserve clause let a club renew a contract for one year only.
Messersmith must stay with the Dodgers forever.
Players must form a new union.
check.why: Seitz read the clause as one renewal year, not an endless chain.

check.q: Under the 1976 agreement, how many years of service did a player need to become a free agent?
check.why: The 1976 agreement set six years of major-league service.

lessons.title: Football and Basketball Follow
lessons.mainIdea: Lawsuits and bargaining brought free agency to basketball in 1976 and to football in 1993, each after years of court fights.
reading: Football never had baseball's exemption. In Radovich v. National Football League (1957), the Supreme Court ruled that pro football was covered by antitrust law. Bill Radovich had been blacklisted after leaving the Detroit Lions for a rival league. A *blacklist* is a list of people that employers agree not to hire.

In basketball, Oscar Robertson, president of the National Basketball Players Association, filed a lawsuit in 1970 against the NBA. It challenged the reserve system and a planned merger with the American Basketball Association. The case was settled in 1976. The *Robertson settlement* opened limited free agency, with compensation still owed to the player's old team.

NFL players went on strike in 1982 and again in 1987. During the 1987 strike, teams played three weeks of games with replacement players. After the strike, the players took the fight to court. In 1992, in McNeil v. National Football League, a jury in Minneapolis found that the league's limits on free agency broke antitrust law.

A new NFL agreement in 1993 created free agency for veterans. In exchange, the players accepted a *salary cap*, a limit on how much each team may spend on player pay. Basketball's salary cap had taken effect earlier, in the 1984–85 season. The trade of free movement for a spending limit became the pattern in football and basketball.

words.d: a list of people that employers agree not to hire
a limit on how much each team may spend on player pay
the 1976 end to Oscar Robertson's lawsuit that began limited free agency in the NBA

look.title: Freedom and a Ceiling
look.text: 1993. NFL veterans can now sign with any team after their contracts end. At the same time, every team must keep its total player pay under one number. A player can choose his employer. He cannot make a team go over the cap to pay him.
look.prompt: What did each side give up in this trade? Why might both sides accept a deal neither fully wanted?

check.q: What did the Supreme Court rule in Radovich v. NFL (1957)?
choices: Football had the same exemption as baseball.
Players must be paid a minimum salary.
Pro football was covered by antitrust law.
check.why: Unlike baseball, football received no exemption.

check.q: Who led the lawsuit that brought limited free agency to the NBA in 1976?
check.why: Oscar Robertson, the players' association president, filed in 1970; it settled in 1976.

check.q: What did NFL players accept in 1993 in exchange for free agency?
check.why: The 1993 agreement paired veteran free agency with a salary cap.

lessons.title: A Canceled World Series
lessons.mainIdea: Fights over free agency and pay led to baseball strikes, including the 1994–95 strike that canceled the World Series for the first time since 1904.
reading: Owners tried several times to limit free agency after 1976. In 1981, players struck for 50 days in the middle of the season over pay owed to teams that lost free agents. The season was split into two halves. In the mid-1980s, owners quietly agreed not to bid for each other's free agents.

Arbitrators ruled that the owners had acted together against free agents in 1985, 1986 and 1987. This was *collusion*, a secret agreement among rivals that the labor contract forbade. In 1990, the owners agreed to pay the players 280 million dollars in damages. The rulings strengthened players' distrust of owners. Owners used lockouts too: in 1990 they kept players out of spring training camps for 32 days.

On August 12, 1994, the players went on strike. The owners wanted a salary cap. On September 14, acting commissioner Bud Selig announced that the rest of the season and the World Series were canceled. There had been no World Series only once before, in 1904, when the New York Giants refused to play.

The strike lasted into 1995. On March 31, 1995, federal judge Sonia Sotomayor issued an *injunction*, a court order, requiring owners to keep the old rules while bargaining went on. The players returned, and the 1995 season started in late April. The strike had lasted 232 days.

words.d: a secret agreement among rivals to act together, such as owners agreeing not to sign free agents
a court order that requires someone to do or stop doing something
when an employer stops work and keeps workers out to press its demands

look.title: Major-League Baseball Strikes
look.cite: MLB and MLBPA records of work stoppages
look.prompt: Which strike was longest, and what was lost because of it? Why might a two-day strike still matter?

check.q: What is collusion?
choices: a court order to return to work
a secret agreement among rivals to act together
check.why: Arbitrators found owners colluded against free agents in 1985–1987.

check.q: Before 1994, when was the only year with no World Series?
check.why: In 1904 the New York Giants refused to play; there was no Series.

check.q: What did Judge Sonia Sotomayor's injunction in March 1995 do?
choices: It made owners keep the old rules while bargaining went on.
check.why: The injunction restored the old rules, and the players returned.

lessons.title: Old Enough to Turn Pro
lessons.mainIdea: Spencer Haywood challenged the NBA's rule barring players until four years after high school, and a 1971 Supreme Court order let him play, opening a hardship route to early entry.
reading: For decades, the NBA would not sign a player until four years after his high school class graduated. The rule kept most players in college, where they played without pay. The rival American Basketball Association, founded in 1967, was less strict. It allowed a *hardship* case, a player who said his family needed him to earn money right away.

Spencer Haywood won an Olympic gold medal with the U.S. basketball team in Mexico City in 1968. He then played one season for the University of Detroit. In 1969 he left college and signed with the ABA's Denver Rockets. He was named both Rookie of the Year and Most Valuable Player of the ABA for the 1969–70 season.

In 1970 Haywood signed with the NBA's Seattle SuperSonics. The NBA said the signing broke its four-year *eligibility rule* and threatened to punish the club. Haywood sued, arguing the rule was an illegal agreement among teams to shut out workers. A federal judge in Los Angeles ordered that he be allowed to play, but an appeals court put that order on hold.

In March 1971, Justice William O. Douglas restored the order in Haywood v. National Basketball Association, and Haywood kept playing for Seattle. The case was settled later that year. The NBA then let underclassmen enter early by claiming hardship. In 2005 the league and its players agreed to a new *age minimum*: from the 2006 draft, players had to be 19 and one year past high school.

words.d: a rule that says who may join a league or team, such as a minimum age or years out of school
a case in which a player says family need requires earning money right away; used to allow early entry
the youngest age at which a league lets a player sign

look.title: Two Leagues, Two Doors
look.text: 1969. A 20-year-old college player is already one of the best in the country. One league will sign him now if he can show hardship. The other says he must wait two more years, playing unpaid in college. The waiting rule was agreed on by team owners, not written into any law.
look.prompt: Whose interests did the four-year rule protect: the colleges, the NBA owners or the players? Why did Haywood argue it was an antitrust problem?

check.q: What did the NBA's old eligibility rule require?
choices: that players wait four years after their high school class graduated
that players finish a college degree
that players first play in the ABA
check.why: The NBA would not sign a player until four years after his high school class graduated.

check.q: Which justice restored the order that let Haywood play in 1971?
check.why: Justice Douglas reinstated the order in Haywood v. National Basketball Association.

check.q: What rule did the NBA and its players agree to in 2005?
choices: players must be 19 and one year past high school
check.why: From the 2006 draft, players had to be 19 and one year removed from high school.

review.q: What did the 1879 reserve agreement allow each club to do?
choices: keep five players from signing with rival clubs
sign any player in the league

review.q: Which ruling gave baseball its antitrust exemption?
choices: Federal Baseball Club v. National League (1922)
review.why: Justice Holmes wrote in 1922 that baseball was not interstate commerce.

review.q: What finally made most major-league baseball players free to change teams?
choices: the Supreme Court in Flood v. Kuhn
the founding of the Players' League
the Seitz arbitration decision and the 1976 agreement
review.why: Seitz read the reserve clause as one year only, and bargaining followed in 1976.

review.q: How was a Negro League player's situation different from a major-league player's before 1946?
choices: Negro League players were bound by an antitrust exemption.
Negro League players had a strong national union.
Negro League contracts were enforced by the commissioner.
No court or commissioner enforced Negro League contracts, so players could jump teams.
review.why: Players like Satchel Paige jumped to better-paying teams, including in 1937.

review.q: What does the Ted Lindsay trade of 1957 show?
